title: Gershwin and Porgy and Bess
summary: He admires Porgy and Bess, thanks Schillinger for enabling it, and declines to guess Gershwin's later direction.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: Were you conscious of Gershwin's writing, particularly conscious of Gershwin's work in those years?

I understand that he is the Schillinger system. For Porgy and Bess I think he used that and I think that's one of the greatest works I've heard in American music. That opera-- is it considered an opera?
I think it is now, yeah. As a matter of fact, he called it an opera. I've got some of the original sheet music for
that, it was called from an opera, but of course most people in those days thought opera was Italian and richly endowed by the Metropolitan and such, and I'm sure they didn't think of it as an opera.

As I was saying, methods-- I can't get along with methods--not that I can't get along, I can't use them to write with. I can't get a method to come out of me. Nevertheless, I thank God that there was a guy like Schillinger who came along and invented this method so that a guy like Gershwin could come along and use his method to produce Porgy and Bess.
I have speculated-- surely not at length, but if Gershwin had lived which musical direction he would have gone--have you ever speculated, can you imagine what he might be doing musically?
No. I think that would be very difficult, with creative people I don't think you can really call the turn they could go.
The possibilities are limitless. It's impossible to think of directions and then, they could just continue where they were.
